title: Meet a Guest Experience Expert in Boston Making Hospitality More Accessible for Everyone
summary: Meet Leah, a Guest Experience Expert in Boston who is helping create a more accessible and welcoming experience for all.
body_text: Name: Leah B. Position: Guest Experience Expert Hotel: Boston Marriott Copley Place Dream destination: Greece. Give me clear blue water with a sandy beach Most used emoji at work: ☕. As in, can you get me some? There is a quiet bravery in asking for help, especially when you are used to proving that you can do things on your own. Leah has been considered legally blind since birth, so she knows what it can feel like to walk into a room and wonder whether asking for help is the right thing to do. “Especially with having a disability, it can be difficult to let yourself be vulnerable because you want to be perceived as having an ‘I can do, I got this’ attitude,” she says. “It can be hard to ask for help or assistance.” That understanding, along with her family’s deep roots in hospitality and her passion for helping people see the abilities of people with disabilities, led Leah to start asking bigger questions about what makes people feel truly welcomed, and what she could make that happen. Beyond her day-to-day role, Leah is also a member of Marriott’s People with Disabilities Associate Resource Group (ARG), where associates can build connections, share experiences, and strengthen a sense of community. You created a disability awareness training that is now part of your hotel’s onboarding experience. When did you realize this was something you wanted to do? I have always known as an adult I wanted to be in a role where I could teach people about the abilities of the disabled. I have a good friend who is almost completely deaf. We joke and say she is my eyes and I am her ears. When I first started working for Marriott, she shared a few hotel experiences she had as a guest with a disability, which got me thinking: Are we as a hotel as accessible as we could be? Courtesy of Leah B. What made you realize there was an opportunity to do more after experiencing your own onboarding? There was a lot of information about inclusion and accommodating disabled guests, but until you have encountered a real-life situation with a guest, you don’t know what to do. How do you engage with a guest who may be in a wheelchair, or a guest who has a service animal? I started asking my front office director and HR how we accommodate different situations. I also researched ADA (Americans with Disabilities Act) guidelines. Then, the HR team asked me how I would feel about building a training program to present to staff. I was thrilled to have the opportunity to create something impactful that means so much to me personally. What do you think has influenced that drive? My older brother and I have been considered legally blind since birth , and as of this moment , there are no corrective measures that can change that. I feel fortunate and grateful that my parents have always instilled in us a strong sense of independence. We were taught it is important to be curious and ask questions, and it is ok to ask for help if you need it. Courtesy of Leah B. Hospitality is part of your family’s story, too. Can you tell us about your parents’ connection to Marriott? They met working at the Marriott Marco Beach hotel in Florida and, before owning their business, they worked at many properties, including the Boston Copley forty years ago. How was your experience when you first started working at Marriott? To be completely honest, I was intimidated to disclose the fact of my disability when I applied. In the past, I had some negative experiences with employers not wanting to assist with accommodations when I disclosed during the interview process. That’s another reason why this work is important to me. When I was offered the job at Boston Copley, I came in with a letter for the leadership team letting them know what I would need for support. For example, I have a large print computer keyboard. I think they were surprised, but they made me feel welcome from the beginning. The leadership at my hotel has been rooting for my success. They know I care about my work, and receiving Host of the Quarter for Q1 was [a proof of that] and an exciting surprise for me. What has been a moment at Marriott that made you think, “This is where I belong?” The first time I presented my training to the executive team, department heads and managers in a morning meeting. I was a bit nervous, even though I knew all the faces there and everyone was very welcoming. After the meeting, I got the sense that others, too, sometimes feel uncomfortable with something they may be holding onto. On that day, I felt a camaraderie, a part of a supportive team. A team on which we can all shine our light. What would you say to others considering a career at Marriott? I would absolutely encourage others to consider a career with Marriott! Change can be difficult, and starting a new job can be scary, but pushing through fear and discomfort is how you grow. I think it is important to know your strengths and your weaknesses. Most importantly, be yourself. We are in the business of making people feel welcomed, and you will be welcomed. → Marriott Is Hiring! Find What You’re Looking For in a Career

title: ZenaTech’s ZenaDrone Begins Testing Phase for Interceptor P-1 Counter-UAS Drone Platform
summary: ZenaDrone begins testing its Interceptor P-1 Counter-UAS drone platform, advancing next-generation defense drone technology.
body_text: Low-cost VTOL autonomous interceptor advances company’s integrated Counter-UAS portfolio and defense system. VANCOUVER, British Columbia, (July 28, 2026) — ZenaTech, Inc. (Nasdaq: ZENA) (FSE: 49Q) (BMV: ZENA) (“ZenaTech”), a technology solution provider specializing in AI (Artificial Intelligence) drone, Drone as a Service (DaaS), enterprise SaaS, and Quantum Computing solutions, today announces that its ZenaDrone subsidiary has commenced the initial flight testing phase of its Interceptor P-1, the Company’s low-cost, one-way autonomous counter-drone platform designed to physically intercept hostile unmanned aerial systems (UAS). The commencement of testing represents a significant step in expanding the Company’s Counter-UAS drone portfolio and integrated defense system. The Interceptor P-1 is designed as a vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL), one-way autonomous interceptor intended to provide an affordable alternative to traditional missile-based drone defense systems and asymmetric warfare combatting drone swarms with multi-million-dollar missiles. “Our engineering team has reached an important milestone as we begin flight testing of the Interceptor P-1,” said Shaun Passley, Ph.D., CEO of ZenaTech. “This program is focused on validating the aircraft’s flight characteristics, autonomous capabilities, and system reliability before advancing to increasingly complex interception exercises. We believe the demand for affordable counter-drone solutions continues to grow globally as military organizations and critical infrastructure operators seek cost-effective methods to defend against rapidly evolving drone threats.” The initial flight test campaign, to be conducted by the ZenaDrone engineering team at the company’s testing range near its Mesa, Arizona facility, will evaluate vertical takeoff and landing performance, high-speed maneuverability, target acquisition and tracking algorithms, guidance controls, and communications reliability. Subsequent phases are expected to include autonomous target pursuit, moving-target intercept exercises, multi-drone operational scenarios, and integration with the Company’s Zena AI Counter-UAS command software. The Interceptor P-1 prototype was first disclosed in March 2026 which included a target selling price of under $5,000 USD, positioning it as a significantly lower-cost alternative to traditional missile-based and laser-based intercept systems for modern asymmetric drone warfare. In April 2026, ZenaTech provided a further update on its expanding defense manufacturing footprint, announcing the registration of Phoenix Aero LLC , a Ukrainian entity based in Lviv, which is being established to support future manufacturing and testing of the Interceptor P-1 and other counter-UAS systems as part of the Company’s EMEA operations. ZenaTech is in the process of setting up this office. The Company believes that low-cost autonomous interceptors will play an increasingly important role in defending military bases, in maritime situations, at airports, energy facilities, government infrastructure, ports, border operations, and other critical assets against hostile drones and drone swarm attacks. The Interceptor P-1 is being engineered to operate as part of ZenaTech’s broader Counter-UAS ecosystem , integrating with the Company’s AI-powered threat detection, classification, and autonomous swarm command software. The complete architecture is intended to enable a single operator to monitor, identify, prioritize, and respond to multiple airborne threats simultaneously using coordinated autonomous interceptor drones. ZenaTech expects to continue expanding the testing program throughout 2026 as development progresses toward future operational demonstrations and customer evaluations. Further updates will be provided as additional milestones are reached. About ZenaTech ZenaTech (Nasdaq: ZENA) (FSE: 49Q) (BMV: ZENA) is a technology company specializing in AI drone, Drone as a Service (DaaS), enterprise SaaS and Quantum Computing solutions for mission-critical applications for business, government and defense. Since 2017, the Company has leveraged its software development expertise and grown its drone design and manufacturing capabilities through ZenaDrone, to innovate and improve customer inspection, monitoring, safety, security, compliance, and surveying processes. With enterprise software customers using branded solutions in law enforcement, government, and industrial sectors, and drones being implemented in these plus agriculture, defense, and logistics sectors, ZenaTech’s portfolio of solutions helps drive speed, accuracy, and cost savings. The Company operates through global offices in North America, Europe, Taiwan, and UAE, and is growing its DaaS business and global network of locations through acquisitions. About ZenaDrone ZenaDrone , a wholly owned subsidiary of ZenaTech, develops and manufactures autonomous drone solutions that can incorporate machine learning software, AI, predictive modeling, Quantum Computing, and other software and hardware innovations. Created to revolutionize the hemp farming sector, its specialization has grown to multifunctional drone solutions for surveying, monitoring, inspection, tracking, process automation, and defense applications. Currently, the ZenaDrone 1000 drone is used for crop management applications and critical field cargo applications in the defense sector, the IQ Nano indoor drone is used for inventory management and security in the warehouse and logistics sectors, the IQ Square is an outdoor drone designed for power washing and inspections use in commercial and government sectors, and the IQ Quad is for land surveys. ZenaDrone operates three global manufacturing facilities in Arizona, Dubai, and Taiwan, and is advancing counter-UAS maritime interceptor drones and an integrated defense system. title: Articulate Rise AI Avatars vs Dedicated AI Video Tools
summary: Compare Articulate Rise AI Avatars with dedicated AI video tools for course workflow, editing, reuse, governance, cost, and production scale.
body_text: Quick answer: Articulate Rise AI Avatars are a strong workflow test when short presenter clips belong inside a Rise course and your team already uses Articulate 360 AI. A dedicated AI video tool is usually the broader test when video must be reused across channels, produced in many formats, managed as a separate library, or edited and localized at scale. Compare approved outputs, not feature labels. Articulate Rise AI video is no longer just a roadmap idea. As of July 22, 2026, Articulate documents AI Avatars in Rise 360 as an active-development Labs feature . That status matters: Articulate explicitly says functionality may evolve, change, or be removed based on feedback and stability. The practical decision is not whether native or dedicated software is universally better. It is whether the video is primarily a component of a Rise lesson or a reusable organizational asset with its own production lifecycle. What Rise 360 AI Avatars currently do Articulate’s official Labs announcement and operating guide is the controlling source for the current feature. It says: AI Avatars must be enabled in Labs, with AI Assistant enabled. The feature is included with an Articulate 360 AI subscription. Generation uses credits, shown before generation. Creators can choose photorealistic or illustrated characters, create or customize a character, select a voice, and enter or AI-generate a script. Avatar videos work in Rise AI blocks and custom blocks. Closed captions are generated automatically unless deselected. Creators can reopen the workspace to update the character, voice, or script. Generated avatar video can be downloaded from playback. Videos are limited to five minutes; Articulate recommends shorter presenter clips for the best results. Articulate positions the feature for short, single-narrator moments such as lesson introductions, transitions, and key takeaways. Its current guide also names known limitations including generation time, unwanted hand motion, unnatural background motion, and endings that may trail off. It states these model limitations cannot currently be fixed through prompt adjustments. Those disclosures make the intended use clear: short presenter inserts, not an assumption that every Rise lesson should become an avatar video. Native Rise AI video: where it has an advantage It reduces context switching The creator can generate a presenter video inside the course authoring environment and continue building while generation runs. In custom blocks, the video can be combined with other objects and resized. This may simplify a workflow in which the final destination is always a Rise lesson. Course context stays visible The instructional designer can judge the avatar clip beside the text, interaction, knowledge check, and surrounding lesson flow. That helps prevent video from becoming a detached production request. Procurement may be simpler for existing customers Teams already licensed for Articulate 360 AI can test the feature within the product they govern. That does not make the incremental cost zero: generation uses credits, creator and reviewer time still matter, and Labs terms need review. Capture the actual credit model and subscription entitlement when making the decision. Illustrated and photorealistic character options Articulate documents both character styles and customization through prompts and reference images. That can be useful when an illustrated visual language fits the course better than a photorealistic presenter. Dedicated AI video tools: where they have an advantage “Dedicated” covers different production models. Synthesia centers presenter-led AI avatar video; Vyond combines AI avatars with editable animation and mixed media; document-to-video products begin with source documents. See Knowlify’s training video software guide for category distinctions. Video exists independently of one course A dedicated platform treats video as the primary asset. That matters when the same approved clip must appear in an LMS, intranet, knowledge base, sales enablement hub, help center, and communication campaign. Rise now supports downloading generated avatar videos, but a team should still test how masters, variants, captions, translations, ownership, and replacement links are managed outside the course. Broader production depth Dedicated products may offer deeper controls for presenter scenes, brand systems, media, collaboration, localization, animation, interactivity, analytics, or enterprise governance. Capabilities and plan entitlements differ. For example, Synthesia’s official features and pricing pages describe plan-dependent avatars, collaboration, translation, brand, interactive, and SCORM functions. Vyond’s plans page documents animation, mixed media, captions, global edits, translation, AI credits, and multiple export formats. Do not infer that a longer feature list produces better training. Test only the capabilities your operating model will use. Video-library production at scale If a centralized media team receives requests from multiple course authors, a dedicated workspace may offer a cleaner separation between course assembly and video production. It can also make reuse and specialist review easier. The trade-off is another vendor, another workflow, and potentially another review link or asset handoff. The decision framework Question Native Rise AI Avatars may fit when… A dedicated tool may fit when… Where will the video live? Mainly inside one Rise course Across courses and non-course channels What format is needed? Short, single-presenter insert Presenter, animation, mixed media, long-form, or multiple formats Who creates it? The course author owns the full lesson A video team or specialist supports many authors How is it updated? Edit and regenerate in course context Update a master asset and distribute versions What must be governed? Existing Articulate workspace and course review Separate video library, permissions, brands, languages, and channels What is the source? A concise approved script Scripts, documents, decks, media, or detailed scenes How much control is required? Character, voice, script, and block placement meet the need Deeper timeline, visual, presenter, animation, or localization controls are required Use a hybrid if the routing rule is explicit. For example: native Rise avatars for short introductions and transitions; dedicated video production for reusable policy modules, complex demonstrations, animated scenarios, or multilingual campaign assets. For document-heavy workflows, compare the category in the 2026 AI training video generator guide , not only avatar products.
